events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Priya proposes Priya, Omar. As team leader, I trust myself and want to test Omar on this first mission to establish a strong start.

I can support testing Priya and Omar on Mission 1. The team is small, and a success here gives us useful information. Priya, as leader, you have explained your trust in yourself and your desire to test Omar; that is a coherent first proposal. I do not see a reason to reject solely for speculation. I will vote based on whether this team stays as proposed. Omar, since you are the new element on this team, can you respond to the specific point of how you will handle the mission card if this team is approved?

Thank you, Theo, for the direct question. I am happy to answer it. If this team of Priya and myself is approved, I will submit a Success card, full stop. I have no hidden agenda on this mission, and I have no reason to want Mission 1 to fail. A first-mission failure would only sow distrust and hand momentum to the enemies of the round table, and I want nothing to do with that. I appreciate Priya's reasoning as leader: a two-person team of the leader plus one other gives us a clean read. If this mission succeeds, both of us gain credibility; if it fails, both of us come under scrutiny, and I accept that trade willingly because I intend to succeed. From my perspective, Priya volunteering to be tested on the very first mission is a positive signal, not a suspicious one. An evil player who knew they might fail a mission would more naturally want to ride along on larger teams where a fail card is harder to attribute, or avoid leadership early. Priya has done the opposite by proposing the smallest possible team with herself on it. As for me, I recognize I am the unknown quantity here, since I was placed on this team by the leader rather than volunteering. That is exactly why I welcome the question about my mission card: I want my answer on record so the result of this mission can be measured against it. I have no information about anyone's alignment, and I make no accusations. I support this proposal as it stands, and I encourage everyone to consider that approving a small, accountable team early is one of the best information-gathering moves available to Good.

I don't have a strong read on either Priya or Omar yet. A successful first mission would be useful, but it wouldn't clear both players, since Evil can choose Success. From my perspective, I'd prefer a team including me, so I'm not ready to support this proposal as it stands.

I remain comfortable with Priya and Omar as proposed. Omar answered the accountability question directly, and Priya has put herself on the smallest possible first team, which is a reasonable information play. Leo, you said you would prefer a team including you; that is a preference, but I want to distinguish it from an objection. Do you intend to vote against this exact Priya–Omar team solely because you are not on it, or do you have a specific concern about either nominee's mission behavior? If it is only a preference, I would ask you to weigh the value of a clean two-person test rather than force a rejection before we have any mission result.

Theo, my objection is based on not being on the team, not on a specific accusation against Priya or Omar. Since I know I would play Success, I prefer a team that includes me. A failure on Priya and Omar would narrow suspicion to those two, but a success would not clear either of them. I’m leaning against this proposal as it stands.

Leo, I appreciate your candor, but you have now confirmed that your objection is not based on a specific concern about Priya or Omar's mission behavior. It is based on your own preference to be included. That is understandable, but it is not enough for me to reject the smallest accountable first-mission test. Omar answered the accountability question directly, and Priya has put herself on the team rather than hiding behind a larger group. A success would not fully clear either of them, as you say, but it still gives us a cleaner baseline than a speculative rejection. I remain comfortable with Priya and Omar as proposed, and if the team stays unchanged, I intend to vote to approve it.

I've been listening carefully, and I think the case for this team is straightforward. Priya, as leader, has put herself on the smallest possible team for Mission 1 — that is a transparent move. If the mission fails, suspicion lands squarely on her and Omar. Evil players typically avoid exposing themselves to that level of scrutiny on the first mission, especially on a two-person team where a fail card is directly attributable.

Omar has made a clear public commitment to Success and welcomed the accountability question from Theo. His reasoning about why Evil would prefer larger teams or avoid leadership early is sound.

Leo, I want to address your position gently: I understand wanting to be on the team since you know you would play Success. But every player can say that about themselves — the statement has no special evidentiary value, and voting against a proposal purely because you are not on it is not a strategy that helps Good find the truth. If Priya and Omar succeed, we gain a baseline. If they fail, we narrow suspicion dramatically. Either outcome moves us forward.

I intend to approve this proposal if it stands as proposed. Let us get Mission 1 done.

Noah, I agree that my own claim of playing Success is not evidence for anyone else. But a successful mission would not clear Priya or Omar, and Evil can also propose or support a small team. I still prefer a team with me on it, and Theo is another option I would consider. Priya, would you consider revising the team to include me, and if not, why keep Omar over me?

Leo, to answer your question directly: no, I will not revise the proposal to swap Omar for you. Omar answered Theo's question clearly and committed to playing Success under full public accountability. Swapping him out simply because you prefer to be on the mission offers no strategic advantage to the town, especially when your objection relies purely on wanting personal inclusion rather than any substantive concern about Omar. Noah and Theo have both indicated they are comfortable with this test, giving us solid support to establish our baseline on Mission 1. I will be keeping the team as Priya and Omar, and I encourage everyone to approve it.

Leo has now stated his position three times, and it has not changed: he wants to be on the team because he knows he would play Success, and he admits there is no specific concern about Priya or me. I want to engage with his strongest point honestly, because he is right about one thing — a successful mission does not clear anyone. Evil can play Success to build credibility. That is true of every team configuration in this game, including any team that includes Leo. A success on a three-person team with Leo on it would be no more informative than a success on this two-person team. So the question is not whether a success fully clears us; it is which proposal gives Good the better information and the better accountability. This team is the smallest possible test. Priya, the leader, has put herself on it. I have publicly committed to a Success card with my name attached, and if this mission fails, suspicion lands on exactly two people — one of whom volunteered to be scrutinized. That is a clean, attributable test. Swapping me for Leo would not improve it: Leo has offered no argument for why his inclusion produces better information, only that he would personally play Success, which as Noah correctly noted is something every player can claim and no one else can verify. I would also gently note the strategic shape of Leo's position. A first-mission team of Priya and me going through gives a crisp result either way. Repeatedly pushing to replace one nominee with himself, while conceding he has no substantive concern about either nominee, is not a play that helps Good find Evil — it is a play that helps Leo build his own resume. I do not accuse him of being Evil for that; self-interest is natural and most people here are Good. But the group should weigh arguments on their merits, and on the merits, nothing Leo has said favors revision. I stand by my commitment, I stand by this team, and I ask everyone to approve Priya and Omar so we can get a real result on the board.

I appreciate how thorough this discussion has been. To summarize where I land: Priya, as leader, put herself on the smallest possible team for Mission 1 — that is transparent and accountable. Omar committed publicly to Success and addressed Theo's question directly. Leo, your desire to be on the team is fair, but as you acknowledged yourself, it is not based on a concern about either nominee's behavior. Omar's latest point is well taken: no mission result fully clears anyone, so the real question is which team gives us the cleanest, most attributable outcome. A two-person team with the leader on it does exactly that.

I intend to approve this proposal if it stands as Priya and Omar. Let us move to the vote.
Priya confirms Priya, Omar. I stand by the proposal of Priya and Omar, as the discussion has built strong consensus for this clean baseline on Mission 1.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Leo proposes Leo, Priya, Theo. Priya was on the successful first mission, and Theo supported that team. I’m including myself because I know I’ll play Success.

I support Leo's proposed team of Leo, Priya, and Theo. Priya was on the Mission 1 team that succeeded and has shown clear reasoning throughout. Leo is now leader and has proposed a three-person team that includes himself, which is accountable and consistent with his earlier stated preference to be included. I am also on this team, and I will submit a Success card. I know my own loyalty, and combining Priya's successful Mission 1 baseline with Leo's accountability and my own commitment gives us a reasonable Mission 2 team. Leo's Mission 1 rejection was based on wanting to be included, and now as leader he has included himself; that is consistent rather than a substantive concern. I see no stronger reason to reject this team, and if it is approved I will do my part to make Mission 2 succeed.

I support Leo's proposed team of Leo, Priya, and Theo for Mission 2. Here's my reasoning:

First, Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards from Priya and Omar. Priya, as leader on Mission 1, put herself on the smallest possible team and it paid off — she has earned a spot on Mission 2. Leo, as the current leader, has included himself on the team, which mirrors Priya's approach of accountability through personal inclusion. Theo has been a consistent, clear voice throughout discussions and has publicly committed to playing Success.

The three-person team for Mission 2 is the standard size for a five-player game, so no structural concerns there. What I appreciate about this proposal is that it builds directly on the trust established in Mission 1 while spreading participation — Priya carried over, Leo joins as leader, and Theo steps up.

Omar, you and I are the two players sitting out this mission. I have no concern about your exclusion from Mission 1's team, and I take Leo's proposal in good faith as a leader including proven and trusted players. The fact that Leo is not shying from scrutiny by putting himself on the team is a positive signal.

I intend to approve this team if it stands as Leo, Priya, and Theo. Let us get Mission 2 done and keep building our momentum toward three successes.

I have serious reservations about this proposal. On Mission 1, Omar and I delivered a clean success with zero fail cards. Furthermore, Leo was the lone player to vote against that team. Now, Leo becomes leader and immediately benches Omar—our only other player with a successful track record—to add both himself and Theo. That means we are introducing two unverified variables onto a critical three-person mission, one of whom actively opposed the mission that just succeeded. Noah, given that you strongly backed Mission 1's clean test, does it not give you pause that we are completely discarding Omar in favor of Leo and Theo simultaneously?

Priya, you asked me directly whether Omar's exclusion gives me pause, and I want to answer honestly: it gives me some pause, but not enough to reject the team outright.

Let me lay out my reasoning. Mission 1 succeeded with Priya and Omar, zero fail cards. That is a real data point, and you are right that Omar is the only player besides you who carries a successful mission result. Benching him in favor of two players without that track record does reduce our collective certainty relative to an alternative that keeps Omar onboard.

However, several considerations pull the other way. First, this is a three-person team and only two players sit out, so someone with a success has to sit regardless — the only way to avoid that would be keeping both Priya and Omar and dropping Leo and Theo entirely, which would exclude the leader. Second, Leo including himself is the same accountability play you modeled on Mission 1; I flagged that as a positive signal in my last statement and I stand by it. Third, Theo has been consistent and clear across both discussions and has publicly committed to Success on this team.

The one thing I would push back on is framing this as Leo actively discarding Omar. With five players and a three-person slot, rotation is inevitable. What matters more is whether Leo will be transparent about why he chose Theo over Omar. So rather than reject, I want to hear that directly.

Leo, Priya's core concern is specific: you benched Omar, Mission 1's other successful player, in favor of Theo. Can you respond to that directly — was Theo chosen over Omar for a strategic reason, or is this rotation simply a consequence of team size?

Noah, I chose Theo because he supported the first team and gave clear reasons for doing so; it was a judgment call, not a concern about Omar. Priya is right that keeping both Mission 1 players would introduce only one new player, and that is a reasonable alternative. But a successful mission does not clear either of them, so I don't think Omar's result makes him decisively safer than Theo. I know I will play Success, and I'm comfortable keeping Leo, Priya, and Theo as proposed.

I remain in support of Leo, Priya, and Theo. Priya’s concern about benching Omar is fair, but it does not make this team unsafe. With five players and a three-person team, at least one Mission 1 success must sit out; Leo, as leader, included himself, which is the same accountability play Priya modeled on Mission 1. Leo’s explanation was a judgment call, not a specific accusation against Omar, and Noah was right to ask for that clarity. I have been consistent across both discussions, I am on this team, and I will submit a Success card. Rejecting now would cost us a proposal without giving a cleaner read than a direct Mission 2 result. I intend to approve Leo, Priya, and Theo if the team stands as proposed.

Noah, I want to clarify an important point regarding your earlier logic: you mentioned that with a three-person team, someone from Mission 1 had to sit out regardless. That is mathematically incorrect. Mission 1 had two players, and Mission 2 requires three. A natural progression would be to keep both Mission 1 players and add exactly one new member. Instead, Leo has gone out of his way to bench Omar, thereby introducing two completely untested players onto this team at the same time: himself and Theo.

Consider the optics of this: Leo was the sole player to vote against Mission 1, which went on to succeed cleanly. The moment Leo gets leadership, he removes Omar—the other half of that success—and slots in Theo, who then immediately rubber-stamps the proposal without a shred of hesitation. Calling that a harmless 'judgment call' does not hold up when we have four proposal attempts left and zero reason to blindly accept two unverified additions.

Omar, you delivered a clean Success on Mission 1 and have now been sidelined by Leo without any valid cause. What is your read on Leo and Theo coordinating to push this team through?

Priya asked for my read directly, so here it is honestly. I do not see coordination between Leo and Theo. Leo gave a specific reason for choosing Theo — Theo supported the first proposal with clear reasoning — and Theo's support of this team is consistent with how he engaged on Mission 1, where he asked the accountability question of me before committing. A rubber stamp would have approved my team without scrutiny; Theo did not do that. That said, Priya is right about one structural point: this team introduces two players without a successful mission result while benching the only other player, besides Priya, who has one. That is a legitimate observation, not a personal attack, and I want to acknowledge it fairly even though it concerns me.

I also want to be transparent about my own position, because I am the player who was benched. I have an obvious incentive to argue for my own inclusion, so I will not do that. What I will say is this: from my seat, the meaningful question is not why I am sitting out, but whether this three-person team gives Good an attributable result. It does. Priya is on it with a clean Mission 1 behind her. If Mission 2 fails, the suspicion falls squarely on Leo and Theo, because Priya's record is established and mine does not change — I would still be the player who delivered a zero-fail mission and was excluded by the person who voted against it. If Mission 2 succeeds, Leo and Theo gain credibility and we go into Mission 3 with a much stronger picture of the table.

Leo, one point of caution before the vote: you rejected Mission 1 on preference grounds, and your explanation for benching me was a judgment call rather than a concern. Both are within bounds, but it means you carry the most scrutiny on this team if it fails, since you assembled it, you lead it, and you had a proven alternative available in keeping both Mission 1 players and adding one. I am not accusing you; I am telling you plainly that the accountability structure of your own proposal puts the weight on you, which is how it should work.

On balance, I lean toward approving this team. Rejecting it now spends one of our proposals without producing any new information, and every alternative configuration has the same fundamental property: someone unproven is on the mission, because only Priya and I carry results and a three-person team cannot be built from two people. The difference between this team and a revision is marginal, and a clean result — either way — teaches us more than another round of speculation. I will play my part wherever I am asked, and my commitment from Mission 1 stands: if I am on a mission, I submit Success. I ask the table to weigh the merits and move to the vote.

I remain in support of Leo, Priya, and Theo. Priya is right that keeping both Mission 1 players and adding one new member was a possible alternative, and I do not dismiss that structural point. But her stronger claim — that Leo and I are coordinating to push this team through — is an inference, not evidence. Leo gave a concrete reason for choosing me: I supported the Mission 1 team with clear reasoning. My support here is also consistent with my earlier behavior, since on Mission 1 I did not rubber-stamp Omar; I directly asked him how he would handle the mission card before committing. I have likewise pressed Leo to explain benching Omar, and he did. That is not blind approval.

On the merits, this team contains Priya, who has a clean Mission 1 result, Leo as leader who has included himself and therefore owns the outcome, and me, and I repeat my public commitment to submit Success. Omar himself acknowledged that rejecting this proposal spends an attempt without producing a cleaner read, and that some unproven player must be on a three-person team because only Priya and Omar carry results. I think that is the correct frame. If this mission fails, Leo and I carry the scrutiny, exactly as accountability should work; if it succeeds, we gain useful information. Priya’s concern is legitimate, but it does not outweigh the value of getting a real Mission 2 result. I intend to approve this team as proposed.

Noah, you noted earlier that benching Omar gave you pause. Omar suggested that rejecting spends an attempt without gaining information, but we must remember that this is proposal 1 with zero rejections on the board. We have four rejections to spare. Early rejections are not wasted; they are Good's primary mechanism to enforce disciplined team composition. Approving Leo's proposal means Good willingly accepts two completely untested players on a three-person mission, while sidelining half of the only successful duo we have, all under the leadership of the sole player who voted against Mission 1. If this team has evil on it, Mission 2 fails and we lose our entire momentum. Why gamble on two unknown variables on the very first proposal when we can easily vote this down and demand a safer composition?

Priya, I want to engage with your argument directly because it has genuine merit, and I want to be honest about where it leads.

You are right on the structural point: keeping both Mission 1 players and adding one new member would introduce only one unproven player instead of two. That is a cleaner composition on paper. And you are right that we have four rejections to spare, so we are not under time pressure.

However, I want to flag something that matters: Omar — the player most directly affected by being benched — himself leaned toward approving this team. He argued that the marginal difference between this configuration and a revision is small, and that some unproven player must always be on a three-person team. That gives me pause about rejecting purely on structural grounds.

There is also an option short of outright rejection: Leo, as leader, can still revise the team before we vote. If your concern is specifically about benching Omar, the cleaner play may be to ask Leo to revise rather than force a rejection that hands leadership to a different player.

Leo, I want to put this to you directly: Priya argues that keeping Priya and Omar together with one additional player is structurally safer because it minimizes unproven variables. Would you consider revising your proposal to include Omar, or do you have a specific reason Theo is the better third member? Your answer will shape where I land on the final vote.

Noah, I considered keeping Priya and Omar together. Their success is useful, but it does not clear either of them. I chose Theo because his scrutiny and support of the first team gave me a reason to trust him; I have no specific concern about Omar. I know I will play Success, and I remain comfortable with Leo, Priya, and Theo. I intend to keep the proposal as it stands.

Leo has now answered Noah's direct question twice, and his answer is consistent: he chose Theo because Theo scrutinized and supported the Mission 1 proposal with clear reasoning, and he has no specific concern about me. He considered keeping both Mission 1 players and declined, which is his prerogative as leader. I accept that at face value.

Let me close my own loop. On Mission 1 I was the unknown quantity, and I answered the accountability question publicly before the vote. The mission succeeded, and my record stands. Now, on Mission 2, I am the benched player, and I said earlier that I would not argue from my own incentive. That remains true. Priya's structural point — that this team introduces two unproven players while sidelining half of the only successful duo — is legitimate, and I acknowledged it when she first raised it. But Leo's refusal to revise does not change the fundamental math: only Priya and I carry results, a three-person team cannot be built from two people, and every configuration must include at least one unproven player. The difference between this team and Priya-plus-Omar-plus-one is real but marginal, and rejecting proposal one with four rejections in hand does not guarantee a better team — it only guarantees a new leader and another round of the same speculation.

The accountability structure of this proposal is what convinces me. Priya is on the team with a clean Mission 1 behind her. Leo assembled the team, leads it, included himself, and passed over a proven alternative — so if this mission fails, the scrutiny lands on him and Theo precisely and heavily, while Priya's record and mine are untouched. Theo has publicly committed to Success, and his engagement across both discussions has been consistent rather than rubber-stamping. That is as attributable as a Mission 2 team can be at this point in the game.

I will add one final note before the vote. Priya, you have pressed hard on coordination between Leo and Theo, and I examined that claim when you asked me directly: the evidence does not support it. Leo gave a concrete reason for choosing Theo, and Theo pressed Leo on the benching question rather than approving blindly. Disagreement about team composition is not evidence of evil, and I would caution everyone against letting a defensible structural preference harden into an accusation without a mission result behind it.

My position is unchanged from my earlier statement: I lean toward approving Leo, Priya, and Theo. A clean result, in either direction, teaches this table more than another rejection cycle, and if it fails, we will know exactly where to look. If the mission succeeds, Leo and Theo gain credibility and we carry three players with results into Mission 3. I am ready to move to the vote.

I have already laid out my position in full, so I will keep this brief. My view has not changed: I lean toward approving Leo, Priya, and Theo. I have examined Priya's structural concern carefully, and while it is legitimate on paper, the alternative she favors still requires adding one unproven player, and the accountability structure of this proposal is already as strong as a Mission 2 team can offer — Priya carries a clean result, Leo assembled and leads the team with himself on it, and Theo has been consistent and publicly committed to Success across both discussions. If this mission fails, scrutiny lands precisely on Leo and Theo; if it succeeds, we enter Mission 3 with three players carrying results. Rejecting the first proposal with four rejections in hand guarantees only a new leader and another round of the same speculation, not a better team. I have no new questions and nothing further to add. I am ready for the vote.
Leo confirms Leo, Priya, Theo. I’m keeping Leo, Priya, and Theo. Priya brings the Mission 1 success, and I trust Theo’s engagement and reasoning.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (2 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Priya. I know I am Good, so I include myself. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards from Priya and me, giving Priya a clean record. Mission 2 failed with 2 fail cards from Leo, Priya, and Theo — since Priya also played on the clean Mission 1 and fought hard against this exact team composition, the strongest read is that Leo and Theo are the two fail cards, and Priya is Good. Avoiding both Leo and Theo, the safest two-person team is Omar and Priya.

Two Fail cards mean two of Leo, Priya, and Theo are Evil, but they do not identify which two. Priya’s Mission 1 success does not clear her: an Evil player can play Success, and her opposition to Mission 2 could provide cover afterward.

Omar, I understand including yourself, but I would prefer Omar and Noah to Omar and Priya. Noah was on neither mission, whereas Priya was on the team that produced two Fail cards. I intend to reject the proposed team.

I will not support the proposed Omar and Priya team as it stands. Omar’s reasoning is understandable, but it treats Priya’s Mission 1 success as stronger evidence than it is. Priya was also on Mission 2, which produced two Fail cards, and a prior Success does not clear anyone because Evil can choose Success. With two Fail cards among Leo, Priya, and me, the failure does not identify which two are Evil. I know I submitted Success on Mission 2, so from my seat the failed mission points toward the other two members, and I cannot vote to put Priya straight back onto Mission 3 without resolving that ambiguity. The cleaner alternative is to use a player with no failed-mission record, such as Noah, alongside one of the Mission 2 members rather than reusing Priya immediately. Omar, your proposal gives Priya another mission while excluding Noah entirely, even though Noah was on neither Mission 1 nor Mission 2 and remains the least entangled in the failure. I am not accusing Omar of anything; as leader he included himself and chose a proven Mission 1 player. But Priya’s presence on the Mission 2 failure makes this team weaker than the alternatives, so I intend to vote against Omar and Priya and would support a revision that avoids reusing the failed Mission 2 team.

I cannot support Omar and Priya as proposed. Priya was on Mission 2, which produced two Fail cards. Her Mission 1 success does not clear her, because Evil can play Success. I know I submitted Success on Mission 2; from my seat, the two Fail cards must have come from the other two members of that team, so Priya remains directly implicated. Omar's argument that Mission 1 clears Priya is too strong. The safer composition is Omar with Noah, who has no Mission 2 failure record, rather than putting Priya straight back on a mission. I am not making a new accusation against Omar; as leader he included himself, which is reasonable. But reusing Priya now is the weakest part of this proposal. I intend to vote against Omar and Priya if it stands unchanged, and I would support a revision replacing Priya with Noah.

I still oppose Omar and Priya. Two Fail cards implicate two members of Leo, Priya, and Theo, but the public result does not establish which two. Priya’s Mission 1 success and her opposition to Mission 2 are evidence to consider, not proof of loyalty. Omar and Noah avoids putting anyone from the two-Fail team on this mission, so I prefer that revision and will reject the current proposal.

Omar, I respect that you included yourself and a Mission 1 success. But I cannot support reusing Priya immediately after Mission 2 produced two Fail cards. The public record is that two of Leo, Priya, and I account for those fails, and from my seat I submitted Success, so I am unwilling to treat Priya’s Mission 1 success as clearing her. Evil can play Success on Mission 1 and then Fail later. Her opposition to Mission 2 is not proof of loyalty; it could be positioning. The cleaner Mission 3 test is to avoid the Mission 2 team entirely and use Noah, who has no failed-mission record, alongside one accountable member. This proposal does the opposite: it gives Priya another mission and excludes Noah. Omar, you say the safest read is Leo and Theo as the two fails, but that is exactly the conclusion the public result does not establish. Noah, if you are weighing this, do you see any evidence that Priya is safer than you for this mission, or would you also prefer a composition that does not immediately recycle a Mission 2 member? I intend to reject Omar and Priya as it stands.

The math on Mission 2 settles more than people are acknowledging. With 5 players there are exactly 2 Evil players in the game. Mission 2 produced 2 fail cards from Leo, Priya, and Theo — meaning both Evil players are among those three. That is not speculation; it is arithmetic. Consequently, Omar and Noah must both be Good, since neither was on Mission 2.

So the question is simply which two of Leo, Priya, and Theo are Evil. Consider the behavioral evidence:

Leo voted against Mission 1 — a team that succeeded cleanly with zero fail cards. He then led Mission 2, which produced two fail cards from his own team. Now he opposes Omar and Priya. His pattern is consistently anti-Good.

Theo immediately rubber-stamped Leo's Mission 1 opposition and then Leo's Mission 2 proposal, and now both Leo and Theo are pushing the exact same alternative — Omar and Noah — in lockstep. That alignment is telling. Two players trying to construct the same alternative team after a mission they were both on failed with two fail cards looks less like independent analysis and more like coordination.

Priya, by contrast, was the lone voice against Mission 2's composition and was the only non-contributor to the two fail cards based on her consistent opposition throughout. Omar and I are both provably Good by the arithmetic above. Omar's proposal of Omar and Priya gives us a two-person team where both players are either provably Good or strongly indicated as Good.

Leo and Theo's unified opposition to this team is exactly what I would expect from the two Evil players trying to avoid a guaranteed-success mission. I support Omar and Priya.

Let me answer the objections to my proposal directly, because the case for Omar and Priya is stronger than Leo and Theo are admitting.

First, the arithmetic Noah laid out is correct and no one has refuted it. Five players means exactly two Evil. Mission 2 produced two Fail cards from a three-person team, and Good players must submit Success. Therefore both Evil players were on Mission 2. That means Omar and Noah are provably Good, and the only open question is which two of Leo, Priya, and Theo hold the Fail cards.

Second, notice something the table should not miss: both Leo and Theo have now claimed, in nearly identical language, that they submitted Success on Mission 2 and that the Fail cards must have come from the other two members. Those claims are mutually exclusive. A three-player team with two Fail cards produced exactly one Success card. At most one of Leo and Theo is telling the truth about his own card. They cannot both be Good — and if both claims are false, they are both Evil. So the honest reading is that at least one, and possibly both, of Leo and Theo is lying to us right now about Mission 2.

Third, weigh Priya's record honestly rather than dismissing it as 'not proof.' She delivered a clean Mission 1. She was the lone vote against Mission 2's composition, and she argued against it before the result was known, spending her political capital on exactly the concern that materialized. If Priya were Evil, opposing that team was a risky and unnecessary play — she could have quietly approved a team guaranteed to contain both Evil players and shared the cover. Instead she fought it and was vindicated by the result. Leo's counter-story — that her opposition could be 'positioning' or 'cover' — is precisely the kind of unfalsifiable claim that lets Evil smear a Good player with no evidence.

Fourth, look at the coordination Noah identified. Leo and Theo are running the same play in lockstep: identical claims about their own Success cards, identical insistence that Priya cannot be trusted, identical push to swap in Noah. My proposal puts two strongly-indicated Good players on Mission 3 for a highly likely success. Leo and Theo both intend to reject it. Ask yourselves why players who claim to be Good would vote down the team with the best chance of succeeding — unless at least one of them needs Evil players on missions to have any chance of failing them.

Theo's alternative of 'one Mission 2 member plus Noah' puts a probable Evil player back on the mission. That is strictly worse for Good than Omar and Priya. I am keeping this team as proposed: Omar and Priya. I ask everyone to approve it and put Mission 3 on the board.

Omar, I did not claim to have submitted Success on Mission 2. Your claim that Theo and I both made that statement is incorrect.

The arithmetic does establish that Omar and Noah are Good: both Evil players were on Mission 2. So why take any risk on Priya when Omar and Noah can guarantee a Success? Priya’s opposition to Mission 2 is evidence, but it does not override a team established by the fail count. I will reject Omar and Priya and support Omar and Noah.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
